judge_assessment.explanation: The mathematics is exactly as the judge describes and I re-checked all of it: 3/8 < 5/8 by equal denominators, 3/5 > 3/8 by equal numerators, 2/9 < 2/4, the missing numerator 24 for 3/5 = ?/40, 21/28 > 20/28, 6/8 = 3/4, the order 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10 over thirtieths, and 15/18 > 14/18 — all correct, and 8(a)'s manual entry carries a real acceptance criterion. But the answer key was scored 4 and its fast-grading bank is close to useless on this particular sheet. Five of the eight rows lose a VERIFIED relation to render_quick_answers._fmt (sympify('<') raises, the except branch returns '---'): rows 1, 2 and 3 are bare em dashes because the relation is those problems' only entry, row 5 reads '—, 21' and row 8 reads '—, 15'. Every one of those dashes is a compare entry that verify.py proved. So on a worksheet whose entire subject is which fraction is bigger, the bank shows the comparison for none of its six comparison items, and row 8's dash sits beside a genuine manual entry on the same problem, which is the exact 'a grader cannot tell verified from nobody-checked-this' confusion. Two further gaps: problem 1 ('write one sentence saying why counting the top numbers is safe here') and problem 3 ('say in a few words what a bigger bottom number really does to the pieces') are open responses with no manual entry — only 8(a) has one. And the prompt asked for planted wrong results to be declared as machine-checked traps: traps exist for the numeric items 4, 5 and 8, but Ben's planted 2/9 > 2/4 in problem 3 is a planted wrong RELATION and carries none, because a trap's value field cannot hold a relation. Finally, on the judge's own extraction note: the '43' style artefacts in the bank are pdftotext reading \\frac{3}{4} bottom-up, not a rendering fault — I confirmed the fractions typeset correctly.

strengths_to_preserve: The sequencing is the lesson: problem 1 gives matching denominators where counting numerators IS safe and asks the child to say why, problem 2 gives matching numerators where the bigger denominator is the smaller fraction, and only then do the find-and-fix items arrive. The key underlines that problem 1 is 'the ONE case where looking at the top numbers alone is safe, and knowing why keeps it from being used everywhere else.'

Problem 5's key does not stop at the answer; it shows the shortcut failing by a hair: '21 beats 20 ... a top-numbers-only reader picks the wrong fraction — by a single twenty-eighth.' A near-miss is far more convincing to a ten-year-old than a lopsided example.

Problem 7's key spells out both wrong orderings the two misconceptions produce — a numerator-only reader answers 2/3, 3/5, 7/10 and a denominator-only reader answers 7/10, 3/5, 2/3, 'which is exactly backwards' — so a grader can diagnose from the child's ordering alone.

The two find-and-fix items attack different halves of the same error: Ben changes nothing but compares denominators (2/9 > 2/4), Cara changes only the denominator when building an equivalent fraction (3/5 → 3/40), and the key's size check for Cara is memorable: '3/5 is a little more than half, and 24/40 is a little more than half too. Cara's 3/40 is nowhere near half.'

Problem 8(a)'s manual entry states what full credit requires rather than a model paragraph to match: 'the idea that the bottom number sets the size of the pieces, and one example where the shortcut gives the wrong answer.'

root_causes.description: render_quick_answers._fmt formats string expecteds by calling bare sympy.sympify; a relation raises and falls back to '---', the same glyph the module uses for a manual-only row. This sheet is the worst case for that bug in the batch: comparison relations are the answers to six of eight problems, so five of eight bank rows are dashes and three of them are dashes and nothing else. The related gap is that the trap mechanism is numeric-only — a trap carries {expr, value} — so a planted wrong RELATION (Ben's 2/9 > 2/4) cannot be declared as a machine-checked trap even though the prompt asks for exactly that.
evidence: verify.json ids 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 each contain a {type: compare, order: relation} entry with expected '<' or '>'.
Reproduced: sympy.sympify('<') raises SympifyError, so scripts/render_quick_answers.py _fmt returns '---'.
verify.json declares traps only on the eval items 4, 5 and 8; problem 3's planted 2/9 > 2/4 has none, and the trap schema in scripts/verify.py expects an expression and a numeric value.

root_causes.description: Only the largest written item (8(a)) was declared manual. Problems 1 and 3 each pair a checkable relation with a short written justification, and the justification was treated as covered by the relation check, so the key gives it no acceptance criterion and the gate chain reports one manual item for a sheet with three written responses.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 1: 'Then write one sentence saying why counting the top numbers is safe here.' problem 3: '... and say in a few words what a bigger bottom number really does to the pieces.'
verify.json declares 'manual' exactly once, on id 8.
The prompt requires 'clearly label any genuinely open response for manual review'.

improvements.title: Five of eight bank rows drop a verified comparison on a worksheet about comparing fractions
improvements.proposed_change: In render_quick_answers._fmt, intercept relation strings before sympify and return '$<$', '$>$', '$=$', '$\le$', '$\ge$', '$\neq$'. Stop overloading '---': keep it for manual-only rows and emit a distinct marker for a value that genuinely cannot be rendered, so 'proved' and 'unchecked' are never the same glyph. Separately, extend the trap schema so a compare entry may declare a planted wrong relation ({desc, relation: '>'}) and verify.py can prove it differs from the verified relation — which is what this prompt asked for on problem 3 and what the numeric-only trap field made impossible. I am raising this above the usual p2 for this case: on a comparison-focused sheet the bug removes the answer from the majority of rows rather than from one.
improvements.regression_test: Render curr-124's verify.json and assert rows '1.~$<$', '2.~$>$', '3.~$<$', '5.~$>$, 21' and '8.~$>$, 15'. All five fail today. Add a trap-schema test: a compare entry declaring relation '>' as a planted wrong answer must verify as distinguishable from the expected '<' and must print under 'Common wrong answers'.
improvements.expected_impact: Turns an almost empty bank into a usable one for the six comparison items, and lets the misconception-analysis mode declare relation traps, which the prompt explicitly required and the schema currently forbids.
improvements.risk: The trap extension changes a validated schema in verify.py, so existing fixtures must keep passing; the rendering half is low-risk and can land first.

improvements.title: Problems 1 and 3 print written justifications with no manual entry
improvements.proposed_change: Require a manual entry for any problem body containing an explanation imperative, including short ones ('write one sentence saying why ...', 'say in a few words ...'), enforced as a gate lint over the worksheet source and stated in SKILL.md. Each declared item should get an acceptance criterion in the key, as 8(a) already does.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture with curr-124's problems 1 and 3 texts and a verify.json declaring manual only on id 8. The lint must name both; adding manual entries must make it pass and must raise the gate summary's manual count from 1 to 3.
improvements.expected_impact: The adult grading this sheet is told that three responses need reading, not one — which matters most here because the written justification is where the misconception actually shows.
improvements.risk: Confine keyword scanning to problem bodies; the directions block on this sheet contains similar phrasing.

case_summary: Pedagogically this is one of the strongest sheets in the batch: the shortcut is met where it works before it is met where it fails, the two find-and-fix items attack the numerator-only and denominator-only errors separately, and problem 5's key shows the shortcut losing by a single twenty-eighth. All eight comparisons are mathematically correct. But the delivered answer key's fast-grading bank shows the comparison for none of the six comparison items: rows 1, 2 and 3 are bare em dashes, rows 5 and 8 open with one, and every one of those dashes is a verified compare relation dropped by _fmt's bare sympify — sitting, on row 8, next to a genuine manual item, which is precisely the confusion that glyph reuse creates. Problems 1 and 3 also print written justifications with no manual entry, and Ben's planted 2/9 > 2/4 could not be declared as a machine-checked trap because the trap schema is numeric-only, so one clause of the prompt was structurally unsatisfiable.
